title: If the world hates you (John 15:18–27)
hookLine: a warning that following him won't always be popular

lines: RECRUITERS SAVE THE HARD PART FOR LATER.
JESUS SAYS IT AT THE TABLE.
cards: Most recruiting pitches lead with the good news: great team, real purpose, benefits from day one. The hard parts come later, in the fine print, if at all.
Jesus has just told his friends they are chosen, loved, let in on the plan. And in the very same breath, he does something no recruiter would do.
He tells them the hard part, plainly, at the table, with no fine print: people will not always like you for this. Some will hate you.

teach.h: KOSMOS: LOVED BY GOD, OFTEN HOSTILE.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you." The world here is the Greek word kosmos, and John uses it in a surprising double way.
In chapter three, God so loved the world. Here, the world hates. Same word.
Here the world seems to mean not the planet or nature or ordinary life, but people and powers organized as if God weren't there. In John's telling, God loves it, and it often doesn't love back.
So the warning isn't that the disciples should hate the world. It's that they shouldn't be shocked when the world pushes against them.

teach.h: THE SERVANT IS NOT GREATER THAN HIS LORD.
teach.b: Then Jesus reminds them of something he said at the foot washing: "The servant is not greater than his lord." If they treated me this way, don't expect better.
And he quotes a line of scripture, one readers find in the Psalms: "They hated me without a cause." There's a comfort folded inside the warning, in that small word before.

teach.h: IT HATED ME FIRST: HE WENT AHEAD.
teach.b: The disciples won't be the first; he has gone through it ahead of them. The passage ends with a promise and a job.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT TESTIFIES, AND SO WILL YOU.
teach.b: The Comforter, the Spirit of truth, will testify, and so will they, "because ye have been with me from the beginning."

teach.h: IT HATED ME BEFORE IT HATED YOU.
teach.b: Christians have read these verses in very different times. Where believers have faced real persecution, in the early centuries and in places today, the words have been a lifeline.
In comfortable places, some readers take them as a warning against two things: seeking approval at any cost, and mistaking ordinary criticism for persecution.

how: Christians in places where faith brings danger often read John 15 as words of courage, and some churches set aside a day each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted.

games.q: you've just told your friends they're chosen and loved. what do you tell them next?
o: that the world may hate them, as it hated you first.
that they should keep it secret.
games.why: he tells them the hard part plainly: "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you."

practice: Think of someone who doesn't like you, a coworker, an in-law, a neighbor, someone online, and notice what happens in your body: the tight jaw, the speech you're already rehearsing; breathe into that.
Then picture one small kindness you could show them anyway, not to win them over, just because kindness doesn't need their approval. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, simply wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Kosmos. The Greek word behind the world, used two ways in John: the world God loves, and the world that hates him.

orig.note: Greek: order, adornment, the world. in John it can mean the world God loves (3:16) and the world that hates him (15:18).
